question_en: An analyst using the Sortino ratio to evaluate an alternative investment is most likely interested in the investment's:
explanation_en:
Alternative investments (eg, hedge funds) often have nonnormal return distributions. The distributions may be negatively skewed or leptokurtic,
both of which indicate the investments have a greater probability of negative returns than implied by a normal distribution.
Standard deviation, the basis of many risk-adjusted return measures (eg, Sharpe ratio), is based on a normal distribution of returns. Given the
nature of standard deviation, downside (eg, very large negative returns) and upside (eg, very large positive returns) volatility are treated equally in
assessing risk.
In contrast, the Sortino ratio measures return relative to downside deviation and incorporates only returns below a minimum return
threshold (eg, risk-free rate, zero) in the risk calculation; in effect, returns below the threshold are the only returns that constitute risk. This ratio is
therefore a more appropriate measure of downside risk. The Sortino ratio can be used as a comparative tool; the investment with the higher
ratio is preferred since it is generating more return per downside risk (ie, unfavorable volatility).
(Choice A) Return relative to total risk is best reflected by the Sharpe ratio, not the Sortino ratio. The Sharpe ratio captures both upside and
downside volatility by using the standard deviation as a risk measure.
(Choice C) Return relative to systematic risk is best reflected by the Treynor ratio, not the Sortino ratio. The Treynor ratio uses beta, a measure
of systematic risk, as its risk measure.

subtopic: 7.07 Yield and Yield Spread Measures for Fixed-Rate Bonds
question_en: A bond has two future cash flows: SAR 5 in 1 year and SAR 105 in 2 years, and the 1- and 2-year benchmark spot rates are 3% and 4% respectively. If the Z-spread is 6%, the bond's price is closest to:
explanation_en:
HP 12c TI BA II Plus
The Z-spread (ie, zero-volatility spread) for a given bond is the yield spread, constant for all of the bond's cash flows, that when added to the
benchmark spot rates and used to discount each of the bond's cash flows, equates the sum of the present values of the cash flows with
the bond's observed price. The Z-spread is the same for all cash flow times-to-maturity for a given bond.
In this scenario, the bond's two future cash flows are SAR 5 in 1 year and SAR 105 in 2 years. The 1- and 2-year benchmark spot rates are 3%
and 4%. Based on the Z-spread of 6%, the bond's price is calculated as:
(Choice B) 92.92 is the result of incorrectly reversing the 1 and 2 year benchmark spot rates in determining the discount rate for each cash flow.
(Choice C) 98.17 is the result of discounting both cash flows by only the Z-spread, and not adding in the benchmark spot rates to obtain the
discount rate for each cash flow.

question_en: Expecting a recession, a portfolio manager changes the allocation in a client's equity portfolio by overweighting consumer staples and utilities while underweighting industrials. The portfolio manager's action is best described as:
explanation_en: Sector rotation is a timing strategy used to reallocate a portfolio based on an investor's perception of the business cycle or other macro variables (eg, oil prices, yield curve shifts). Sector rotation is a common technique used by practitioners in an attempt to outperform their benchmarks and is a common application of industry analysis. A cyclical industry is highly correlated to the strength of the overall economy, while a noncyclical industry is more insulated from economic fluctuations. By shifting away from cyclical stocks (eg, industrials) and into noncyclical stocks (eg, consumer staples, utilities), the manager is attempting to reduce the negative effects of a recession on the portfolio. (Choice A) Risk budgeting measures and allocates risks by specific portfolio metrics (eg, beta), often limiting the total risk of the portfolio to a predetermined "budget." Although the portfolio's overall risk was likely reduced by the sector shifts, it was done on an ad hoc basis and nothing in the question implied that the portfolio was adhering to or constrained by a risk budget. (Choice C) Tactical asset allocation refers to tactical shifts among various asset classes (eg, equities, fixed income), not within an asset class.

subtopic: 11.01 Ethics And Trust in the Investment Profession
question_en: An investment professional least likely displays a high level of professionalism when:
option_b: working late to help a co-worker finish a project.
option_c: researching the efficacy of a new analytical model.
explanation_en: A profession is an occupation that has an established body of knowledge and standards of practice and behavior. Relative to craft guilds and trade bodies, a profession holds itself to a higher ethical standard. A profession's primary goal is to establish trust between clients and society in general. Examples of professions include doctors, lawyers, and accountants. Characteristics of a profession include Service to clients and society Standardized practitioner behavior High entry standards Body of expert knowledge Encouraging and facilitating continuing education Professional conduct monitoring Recognized governing body Member engagement Collegiality By adhering to the tenets of a profession and by establishing shared principles that all members of the profession agree to and live by, investment professionals build credibility, respect, and trust with clients and society. A profession maintains trust by establishing minimum standards of care that ensure a culture of integrity and competency in practice. In this instance, an investment professional has a duty to their employer, but not at the expense of their clients. The standard of care for an investment professional is a fiduciary standard. This requires acting in the client's best interest, which will not always allow for maximizing firm revenue. (Choice B) Working late to help a co-worker finish a project is an example of collegiality. (Choice C) Researching the efficacy of a new analytical model is a form of continuing education.

question_en: The repo margin in a repurchase agreement refers to the:
option_a: annualized percentage return to the lender of funds. dierence between the purchase price and market price of the underlying
option_b: bond. dierence between the purchase price and the repurchase price of the underlying
explanation_en: The repo margin is the difference between the amount the lender of funds (buyer of the underlying bond) pays for it and its market price or value. This margin offers protection to the repo lender if the value of the bond decreases over the term of the repo agreement.

question_en: Long-term shifts in population from one country to a neighboring country are best described as which type of geopolitical risk?
explanation_en: Geopolitical risks represent the possibility of things occurring which negatively impact peaceful international relations. Population shifts occur over long periods of time, which is indicative of a thematic risk. Event risk relates to the unknown outcome of specific events where the occurrence date is known. Exogenous risk is related to unanticipated events.

question_en:
An analyst gathers the following data for a company:

| Selected Financial Data | CNY millions |
|---|---|
| Credit sales | 15,000 |
| Cost of goods sold | 12,000 |
| Accounts receivable | 2,000 |
| Inventory, beginning balance | 1,500 |
| Inventory, ending balance | 1,000 |
| Accounts payable | 3,000 |

Based on this information, the days of inventory on hand (DOH) is closest to:
explanation_en: Days of inventory on hand (DOH), also referred to as number of days of inventory, measures the average number of days it takes a company to sell its inventory. DOH is an activity ratio that indicates management's effectiveness in managing its inventory, with fewer days usually indicating more efficiency as capital is tied up in inventory for a shorter time. DOH is particularly useful as a means of contrasting operating and asset efficiency when comparing similar businesses. DOH is calculated as average inventory for the period divided by daily COGS. In this case, DOH equals 48.7. (Choice A) 36.5 is credit sales, not average inventory, divided by daily COGS. (Choice B) 40.6 is ending inventory, not average inventory, divided by daily COGS.

question_en: An investor buys 2,000 shares of a stock at $21 per share and deposits an initial margin of 40% of the purchase. If the maintenance margin is 25%, the trigger price for a margin call is closest to:
explanation_en:
A trader may buy stock in a margin account and pay for only part of the position's purchase price in cash. The rest of the purchase is financed
using a margin loan extended by the broker-dealer. This is referred to as "buying on margin."
Margin accounts have an initial margin requirement and a maintenance margin requirement. The initial margin requirement may be set by the
government, the exchange, or the clearinghouse. Broker-dealers who accept margin accounts typically set the minimum margin requirement at
25%, but they may set it higher or lower depending on the position's volatility and their individual policies. The trader will get a margin call if the
position equity falls below the maintenance margin requirement, which happens when the stock price falls below the trigger price, P .
T
In this scenario, the initial share price is $21. Since the initial margin requirement is 40%, the trader uses (21 × 0.40 =) $8.40 per share in cash to
make the purchase. Maintenance margin expressed as a decimal is 0.25. Substitute into the formula above to calculate the trigger price:
(Choice B) $13.13 is the result of multiplying the purchase price by the ratio of the maintenance margin to the initial margin requirement.
(Choice C) $17.85 is the result of calculating a share price 15% below the initial purchase price based on the 15% difference in the initial margin
and maintenance margin requirements.

subtopic: Reading 21 Portfolio Risk and Return Part II
question_en: In Fama and French's multifactor model, the expected return on a stock is explained by: excess return on the market portfolio, book-to-market ratio, and price
option_b: rm size, book-to-market ratio, and excess return on the market portfolio.
option_c: rm size, book-to-market ratio, and price momentum.
explanation_en: In the Fama and French model, the three factors that explain individual stock returns are firm size, the firm's book value-to-market value ratio, and the excess return on the market portfolio. The Carhart model added price momentum as a fourth factor.

question_en: With regards to credit analysis, management's strategy and execution most likely affects:
explanation_en: 4 Cs of credit analysis Capacity Ability to make debt payments on time Collateral Value of assets supporting debt Covenants Terms and conditions in debt contracts Character Track record of management Capacity is a borrower's ability to service debt. Evaluating capacity entails both industry and company analysis. The industries in which a borrower operates are analyzed to understand the competitive environment and prospects for growth and how each impacts borrower cash flow. Beyond assessing the general operating environment, borrower-specific circumstances are analyzed, including: Ability to generate revenue (eg, sales trends and turnover ratios) Profitability (eg, profit margins and return ratios Solvency and ability to meet obligations (eg, debt ratios and coverage ratios) Operating and financial leverage EBITDA is a proxy for operating cash flow. EBITDA/interest expense is a widely used coverage ratio. Beyond operating considerations, capacity is also influenced by the ability to obtain additional funds (eg, access to capital markets or banks). (Choice A) Management's track record is addressed in Character. (Choice C) Asset values versus level of indebtedness is addressed under Collateral.

subtopic: 7.09 The Term Structure of Interest Rates Spot, Par, and Forward Curves
question_en: An investor wants to price a two-year, 6% annual coupon bond. Spot rates are 5% for zero-coupon, one-year bonds of similar credit quality and 7% for similar, zero-coupon, two-year bonds. Based on this information, the price of the bond per 100 of par value is closest to:
explanation_en:
HP 12c TI BA II Plus
A coupon-paying bond can be conceptualized as a series of zero-coupon bonds. Each cash flow is identical to a zero-coupon bond that has a
face value equal to the cash flow and matures at the time of the payment. The present value (ie, price) of any zero-coupon bond is its face value
discounted by its spot rate.
This leads to the "no-arbitrage" rule for pricing bonds. Since any cash flow of a coupon-paying bond is economically equivalent to its
corresponding zero-coupon bond, both must have the same value. Any discrepancy allows an investor to realize riskless arbitrage profits. To
prevent arbitrage, each cash flow must be discounted at the same rate as for a zero-coupon bond of the same maturity (eg, the spot rate for that
maturity).
The sum of the present values for all cash flows is the "no-arbitrage" price of the bond. The calculations are shown below:
(Choice A) 98.19 is the present value from using 7% as the discount rate for both the bonds' cash flows.
(Choice C) 101.86 results from using 5% as the discount rate for both the bonds' cash flows.

question_en: A company which runs testing on lab samples offers the following pricing: Samples 1 – 100: $6 per sample Samples 101 – 200: $4 per sample Samples 201 – 300: $3 per sample This structure is an example of:
explanation_en: Tiered pricing is based on volume of purchases. Dynamic pricing offers different prices at different times. Add-on pricing involves additional options that can be included with a product.

question_en: Financial intermediaries that issue securities which represent interests in a pool of similar financial assets are best characterized as:
explanation_en: Securitizers are financial intermediaries that assemble large pools of similar financial assets, such as mortgages or loans, and issue securities that represent interests in the pool. Block brokers assist their clients with large trades of securities. Arbitrageurs simultaneously buy and sell the same asset in different markets to take advantage of different prices for the same asset.
